claims.text: The target Mg-containing lightweight HEA has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The initial non-equilibrium microstructure contains a solid-solution matrix together with intermetallic compounds.
The dispersed intermetallic compounds are metastable and contain Mg.
Thermal exposure causes localized Mg segregation in the metastable microstructure.
Metastable phases promote Mg diffusion and segregation toward the surface at high temperature.
Several hours of sub-melting high-temperature exposure permits significant Mg diffusion.
Mg segregation produces micron-scale Mg-rich regions.
Surface-segregated Mg reacts with oxygen to form a continuous, dense MgO-rich surface scale.
An oxide-rich surface scale can passivate an Mg-containing alloy and reduce corrosion or oxidation-related degradation.
The continuous MgO-rich scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial as-cast state.
Spatial heterogeneity in Mg content creates compositional gradients that act as microgalvanic couples.
The proposed microgalvanic couples intensify localized corrosion where the protective oxide is incomplete or disrupted.
Regions exhibiting pronounced Mg segregation will have higher localized corrosion rates than the initial non-equilibrium baseline.
Mg-rich multielement alloy systems remain poorly understood with respect to phase stability and passivation behavior.
The kinetics of Mg diffusion and MgO-scale formation depend on alloy composition and processing history.
The magnitude of the proposed galvanic driving force depends on alloy composition and processing history.
The mechanism applies only below incipient melting, where Mg diffusion can occur without melting the alloy.
